newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Warring Afghans say they're ready for ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Warring Afghans say they're ready for ceasefire.

text.p: Afghanistan's radical Islamic Taleban and their opponents said on Monday they were ready to accept a Pakistani-brokered ceasefire, but the two sides set contrasting conditions.

The Taleban, who control Kabul, and forces loyal to ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood battling for control of the plain north of the capital, traded sporadic tank, artillery and rocket fire, but there were no signs of an immediate offensive by either side.

Dr Abdullah, a spokesman for Masood, said in the town of Jabal os-Siraj, 70 km (45 miles) north of Kabul, that the ceasefire was acceptable, but only on condition that the Afghan capital be demilitarised afterwards.
"If a ceasefire is agreed today, then talks on the demilitarisation of Kabul should start immediately," he said.
A Taleban spokesman in the southern city of Kandahar said the militia had agreed to a ceasefire, but insisted that it must be followed immediately by an exchange of prisoners.

The spokesman, Syed Mohammed Haqqani, said the Taleban wanted the truce monitored by a 12-man commission. The Taleban would choose six of its members, while the rest would come from opposed factions, including those of Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum, Masood and Shi'ite Moslem leader Karim Khalili.
If the ceasefire held, and prisoners were exchanged, peace talks could follow, Haqqani said.

Taleban sources said Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar, who conveyed the ceasefire proposal to the Taleban on Sunday, had flown back to the Dostum-held northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif from Kandahar on Monday.
He was planning to transmit the Taleban's acceptance of the ceasefire, due to take effect at midday (0730 GMT).
Babar has been shuttling between Kandahar and Mazar-i-Sharif to try to prevent fighting between the Taleban, who captured Kabul on September 27, and Dostum's Uzbek forces.
Pakistan denies charges by the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani that it supports the Taleban.

Earlier on Monday, Masood's forces lobbed rockets and shells at Taleban positions along the new road which leads into northeastern Kabul. There was little return fire, save a shell that smacked into a government position in the village of Hussein Kot, 15 km (10 miles) north of the capital.
Taleban fighters in Hussein Kot told a Reuters correspondent that they had retaken two hills from Masood's fighters, but were meeting resistance from villages behind their front line.

The Taleban's official radio said their militia had rolled back Masood's forces and retrieved several arms caches in areas west of Kabul. It said the weapons included eight U.S.-made Stinger surface-to-air missiles.

Masood, strengthened by a new alliance with his former rival Dostum, had captured Bagram air base, 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul on Friday. By Sunday his forces were close enough to fire rockets at Kabul airport on the northeast edge of the capital.
But the purist Islamic warriors drove Masood's mainly ethnic Tajik forces back several km (miles) from Kabul later that day.

For the past week fighting has raged around a 30-km (20-mile) stretch of the main road from the capital to the Hindu Kush strongholds of Masood and Dostum, leaving a trail of destruction and refugees in its wake.
The road north of Kabul was empty of traffic for another day on Monday except for Taleban pickups, tanks and the occasional truck loaded with families fleeing from nearby villages.
Morale appeared high amongst Masood's men, who were keen to make a push for the capital they lost less than a month ago.
"We want to go forward," said one fighter, shouldering a rocket-propelled grenade launcher in a crowd of troops oustide Masood's headquarters in Jabal os-Siraj.

Asked what Masood would do if the Taleban refused to allow Kabul to be demilitarised, Abdullah said: "What is their chance of staying in Kabul? They have no support from the people, they are under great pressure militarily, they have losses."
